title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest leans into fresh angles across your tracked topics — where longevity compounds actually move the needle vs. just biomarkers, HIIT's effects on the heart itself, supervised vs. DIY pelvic floor training, vitamin D and exercise as add-ons in HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and why sleep *regularity* may matter more than sleep *duration*. Sources from PubMed, JAMA Network, NIH/ClinicalTrials.gov, Nature, Springer, and AASM are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
Today's theme: separate **biomarker engagement** (moving a lab value) from **clinical benefit** (feeling or functioning better). Several longevity interventions clearly do the former; the latter is still catching up.

- **Rapamycin — longest human data so far.** The **PEARL** trial (NCT04488601), the longest RCT of rapamycin for healthy aging to date, gave placebo, 5 mg, or 10 mg **weekly** for 48 weeks. Intermittent low-dose rapamycin was **relatively safe**, with significant gains in **lean tissue mass and reduced pain in women** — but it did not broadly reverse aging. Two dose-finding trials, **RESTOR** (NCT06658093) and **RAP PAC** (NCT05949658), are now defining safe geroprotective doses, notably testing **sex-specific dosing**.
- **NAD⁺ boosters: the lab value moves, the outcomes don't (yet).** A 2025 *Nature Metabolism* RCT (65 adults) showed **NR and NMN — but not plain nicotinamide — comparably raise circulating NAD⁺** over 14 days. But a PRISMA review of 33 human trials found healthspan outcomes are **heterogeneous or null**, and a 2026 *Alzheimer's & Dementia* RCT found NR **doubled NAD⁺ yet did not improve cognition** in mild cognitive impairment. Target engagement ≠ benefit.
- **Taurine.** The **TauAge** RCT (NCT06613542, TU Munich; completed Nov 2025) tested **4 g/day taurine for 6 months** in adults 55–75 against epigenetic-clock and fitness endpoints — results are awaited and worth watching given mixed prior human data.
- **Skin (procedures/topicals).** A 100-person RCT found **exosome therapy delivered by microneedling outperformed platelet-rich plasma (PRP)** on aesthetic-improvement scores with better tolerability, and a 2026 *Life* RCT showed **laser-assisted exosome boosters** improved short-term scar and skin-quality measures. Note the caveats: small trials, short follow-up, and **senolytic "anti-aging" microneedles remain preclinical**.

Practical framing: favor interventions with **functional** human endpoints, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-compound "longevity" claims with skepticism.

sections.body:
New 2026 evidence extends HIIT's benefits from the scale and VO₂max to the **heart muscle itself** and to specific **cardiometabolic markers**.

- **Cardiac function.** An *International Journal of Obesity* RCT randomized women with obesity to 8 weeks of **HIIT (4×4 min at 85–95% HRmax)** or moderate continuous training (MICT). Both improved myocardial deformation, but **only HIIT improved myocardial efficiency** (less "wasted work," higher work efficiency) — hinting at an edge for reversing subclinical cardiac strain.
- **PCOS.** A network meta-analysis of exercise modes in women with PCOS ranked **HIIT best for lowering fasting insulin, HOMA-IR (insulin resistance), and LDL**, while **combined (aerobic + resistance) training** was best for triglycerides and LDL, and aerobic training best for CRP. A blended week can cover multiple targets.
- **Weight status & age.** A 2026 meta-analysis (15 RCTs, women with overweight/obesity) found HIIT **reduced body weight, BMI, body-fat %, and fat mass and raised VO₂max**, nudging HDL up and LDL down. A separate 2026 synthesis found **age modifies the triglyceride response**, relevant across the menopausal transition.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio, cardiac, and metabolic wins — **pair HIIT with resistance training**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). This week's studies quantify *how much supervision matters* and show PFMT's reach **before surgery** and **during pregnancy**.

- **Supervised beats DIY.** A 2026 RCT (60 women) directly compared **supervised vs. unsupervised home PFMT**. The supervised group's pad-test leakage dropped from **22.89 g → 3.24 g** (vs. 25.71 g → 17.82 g unsupervised), **66.7% reached Oxford grade 4–5** strength (vs. 13.3%), and daily leak episodes fell from **7.63 → 1.69** (vs. 8.88 → 7.75). Unsupervised PFMT still helps *if* adherence is high — but coaching clearly amplifies results.
- **PFMT can defer surgery.** A 2026 *International Urogynecology Journal* RCT of **6-week intensive preoperative PFMT** in women awaiting mid-urethral sling surgery showed large gains in muscle strength (d=0.85) and symptom severity (d=0.90) — and **43% postponed their planned operation**, supporting structured PFMT as a low-risk first step.
- **Prevention in pregnancy.** A multicenter *JAMA Network Open* RCT (764 first-time mothers) found a **pelvic-floor workout (PFMT + postural exercise, "PEFLOW")** during pregnancy cut SUI at 6 weeks postpartum (**8.7% vs. 13.9%**) and roughly doubled the share with strong contractions (**17.8% vs. 7.9%**).

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps** — confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback, and lean toward supervised programs when possible.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard HER2-targeted treatment** — not a replacement for it. Two themes stand out this week.

- **Correcting vitamin D deficiency (with a TP53 angle).** A 2026 *Nutrients* retrospective interventional study of 196 curative-intent **HER2+** patients found that **failing to correct** a vitamin D deficiency carried a **1.7× higher recurrence risk**, while those who repleted trended toward better 3-year disease-free survival (**90% vs. 85%**), with the best outcomes at the highest D levels. The mechanistic hook is **TP53–vitamin D receptor cross-talk**: HER2+ tumors carry TP53 mutations **55–75%** of the time, germline TP53 carriers disproportionately develop HER2+ disease, and in a **TP53-mutated** subset of the AMATERASU trial, vitamin D raised 5-year relapse-free survival to **81% vs. 31%** (HR 0.27).
- **Exercise as supportive care.** A 2026 *Lancet Healthy Longevity* meta-analysis (21 RCTs, ~3,024 women) found exercise **during chemotherapy meaningfully improves quality of life** (aerobic, combined, and strength all worked), and a 2026 *BMC Cancer* meta-analysis showed aerobic exercise **reduces cancer-related fatigue and improves HRQoL**. Importantly, the **Neo-train** RCT found supervised exercise did **not** shrink tumors or change pathologic complete response — but it **improved chemo dose intensity, reduced delays, and shortened hospital stays**. So: better tolerance, not a tumor-killing substitute.

Important framing: much of this is **observational or supportive-care** evidence. Use integrative options as **add-ons discussed with your oncology team** — and coordinate any supplement, since interactions with targeted therapy are real.

sections.body:
For **restless or disjointed** sleep, 2026 evidence keeps sharpening one message: **when** you sleep — and how *consistently* — may matter as much as **how long**.

- **Regularity is its own risk factor.** A 2026 *BMC Cardiovascular Disorders* cohort (Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966) found that **irregular sleep timing** in midlife predicted **major adverse cardiac events and cardiovascular death** over 10 years. This echoes large UK Biobank accelerometer studies where **irregular sleepers had ~26% higher MACE risk** and where the **Sleep Regularity Index predicted mortality more strongly than sleep duration**. Notably, hitting recommended sleep *duration* offset risk for *moderately* irregular sleepers but **not** for the most irregular — so a steady schedule is not optional.
- **Behavior first.** CBT-I remains **first-line** for chronic insomnia (AASM). The 2026 AASM combination-therapy guideline found **CBT-I + medication beats medication alone**, but is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — reinforcing behavioral therapy as the durable core.
- **Supplements, honestly.** A 2025 RCT of **magnesium bisglycinate** (250 mg elemental Mg + glycine daily, 4 weeks, 155 poor sleepers) found a **small but statistically significant** drop in Insomnia Severity Index (effect size d≈0.2), well tolerated. **Melatonin** is best reserved for **circadian issues** (jet lag, shift work), not chronic insomnia.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Anchor a **fixed wake time and bedtime** — 7 days a week (regularity > duration).
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disrupted sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
